summary: This RFC describes a method adopted by CSNET, the VAN gateway, and other organizations for carrying IP datagrams across X.25-based public data networks. It was later replaced by RFC 1356.

eli5.summary: Public data networks only knew how to carry their own kind of parcel. This note explains how to pack Internet letters inside those parcels so they travel safely.

questions: how to send ip datagrams over x.25
how to send ip over x.25
subtitle: How CSNET, the VAN gateway and others carried IP datagrams over X.25 public data networks.

tldr.problem: Public data networks based on X.25 offered virtual circuits, not datagrams, so IP needed an agreed way to ride on them.
tldr.mechanism: An X.25 virtual circuit is opened on demand when a datagram arrives. The first Call User Data octet is hex CC to mean Internet Protocol, and each datagram is sent as a complete packet sequence using the M bit.
tldr.outcome: The standard was adopted by CSNET, the VAN gateway and other organizations. It was replaced by RFC 1356.

today: RFC 877 has been obsoleted by RFC 1356, so it is no longer the current definition of IP over X.25.

sections.title: IP over X.25 Virtual Circuits
sections.content: RFC 877 specifies a standard adopted by CSNET, the VAN gateway and other organizations for sending IP datagrams over X.25-based public data networks. A virtual circuit is opened on demand when a datagram arrives at the network interface, and it is closed after a period of inactivity that depends on the cost of an open circuit. It can also be closed if the interface runs out of circuits.
sections.eli5: When a letter needs to go, the sender opens a private pipe. When the pipe sits idle too long, it is closed to save money.

sections.title: Packing Datagrams into X.25
sections.content:
The first octet in the Call User Data field of the Call Request packet is used for protocol demultiplexing. The value hex CC (binary 11001100, decimal 204) means Internet Protocol. IP datagrams are sent as X.25 complete packet sequences: a datagram begins on a packet boundary and the M (more data) bit is used when it is larger than one packet. There are no additional headers or data in the packets.

Unless a larger packet size is negotiated, the maximum IP datagram size is 576 octets. If two sites negotiate a large X.25 packet size such as 1024 octets, a datagram of that size is allowed.
sections.eli5: The first thing in the call says 'this carries Internet mail'. A long letter is sent in pieces, each marked 'more is coming' until the last one.

sections.title: Closing Circuits
sections.content: Either site may close a virtual circuit. If the circuit is closed or reset while a datagram is being sent, that datagram is lost. Some sites, such as CSNET sites, may try to open several circuits to one site, and the RFC says sites should handle such incoming calls gracefully: transmit on the extra circuits if possible and accept datagrams from them, rather than accepting the call and then closing it or ignoring the datagrams.
sections.eli5: Either side can hang up the pipe. A letter in the middle of travelling when that happens is lost.

sections.title: General Remarks
sections.content: Protocols above IP, such as TCP, do not affect this standard, and no attempt is made to open virtual circuits to match TCP connections. X.25 features not discussed are not used; for example, interrupt packets and the D bit are not used. Negotiable X.25 features are allowed, and sites may negotiate larger packet and window sizes.
sections.eli5: The pipe does not care what is inside the letters. Only the few X.25 features this note mentions are used, and the rest are left alone.

references.text: Comer, D.E. and Korb, J.T., "CSNET Protocol Software: The IP-to-X.25 Interface", SIGCOMM Symposium on Communications Architectures and Protocols, March 1983.
